growth_story.headline: Cyclones, a pandemic, an airline collapse and an earthquake have set Vanuatu back again and again, and income per person is still below its 1979 level.
growth_story.arc: Since 1990 Vanuatu's income per person has grown about 0.5 percent a year with no lasting change of pace, and in 2025 it was still a little below its level in 1979, the first year of the record. Within that long flat line, gains were repeatedly undone: income per person fell 5.8 percent in 2001 and 7.5 percent in 2002, then rose through the mid-2000s, by 5.9 percent in 2006, when the ADB describes fast growth driven by tourism, construction and aid. Growth averaged 0.9 percent a year over 2006–2015 and slowed to 0.2 percent over 2016–2025. Income per person peaked in 2019, then fell 7.9 percent in 2020 and 3.4 percent in 2021 as the pandemic border closure brought tourism to a near stop and Cyclone Harold struck. It recovered by 3.2 percent in 2022 and 3.4 percent in 2023, but three severe cyclones in 2023, the liquidation of Air Vanuatu in 2024 and the Port Vila earthquake in December 2024 weighed on activity. Income per person grew 1.4 percent in 2024 and 0.8 percent in 2025 and remains 3.0 percent below its 2019 peak.

threads.title: Disasters that undo gains
threads.text: Large disasters have hit Vanuatu again and again. Cyclone Pam in 2015 destroyed a large share of the country's housing, crops and tourist facilities, and the December 2024 earthquake in Port Vila followed three severe cyclones in 2023. World Bank phone surveys found that jobs in Shefa, the province that holds the capital, were still below pre-quake levels in mid-2025.

threads.text: Air Vanuatu, the national airline, was liquidated in May 2024 and its international flights stopped, disrupting tourism. The IMF expected these travel disruptions to have slowed growth in 2024. In 2025 air arrivals rose sharply, but cruise arrivals fell.

threads.title: Workers leaving for seasonal jobs
threads.text: A growing number of workers from Vanuatu take seasonal jobs in Australia and New Zealand. The IMF links this to fewer workers and farmers on the land and a loss of skills in key sectors at home, and lists skills shortages among the country's main risks.

threads.title: Pandemic border closure
threads.text: When the borders closed in 2020, tourism came to a near halt and building projects were delayed, while Cyclone Harold and a volcanic eruption on Tanna caused heavy damage. Income per person fell 7.9 percent in 2020, the deepest fall in any year since 1980, and a further 3.4 percent in 2021.

citations.title: IMF Staff Concludes 2021 Article IV Mission to Vanuatu

threads.title: A boom on aid and building
threads.text: After a decade of slow growth, the economy expanded quickly from 2003 to 2008 on tourism, construction and aid inflows. Investment rose to 40.4 percent of GDP in 2008, then fell back to 15.0 percent by 2014.

since_last_year.text: The economy held up through 2025 after the earthquake. The ADB credits tourism, government support and rebuilding, though cruise visits stayed low because of earthquake damage in Port Vila. In September 2025 the IMF lowered Vanuatu's external risk of debt distress after Air Vanuatu's debt restructuring was resolved. Income per person grew 0.8 percent in 2025.

growth_story.tension: The sources describe booms and resilience that income per person barely shows. The ADB counted Vanuatu among the fastest-growing economies in the Pacific in 2003–2008, yet income per person rose only 0.4 percent in 2007; part of the gap is that the population was growing. For 2025 the ADB describes resilient growth, but income per person rose just 0.8 percent. The sources also disagree with each other: the ADB estimates that the economy grew as fast in 2024 as in 2025, while the IMF expected growth in 2024 to have slowed. The ADB notes that Vanuatu changed how it measures growth in 2023, which shifted growth rates slightly for some years.
